label_guide.label: Slippery Slope
label_guide.description: A small first step is claimed to inevitably lead to an extreme chain of consequences, without evidence.

label_guide.label: Appeal to Authority
label_guide.description: A claim is accepted because an authority, expert or celebrity said so, instead of on evidence.

label_guide.label: Bandwagon / Popularity
label_guide.description: Something is claimed true or good because many people believe or do it.

label_guide.label: Hasty Generalization
label_guide.description: A broad conclusion is drawn from a small or unrepresentative sample.

label_guide.label: False Cause / Causality
label_guide.description: Assuming one event caused another just because they are correlated or one followed the other.

label_guide.label: Appeal to Emotion
label_guide.description: Using fear, pity, guilt, anger etc. in place of valid reasons to persuade.

label_guide.label: Composition
label_guide.description: Assuming what is true of the parts must be true of the whole (or of the group).

label_guide.label: False Dilemma
label_guide.description: Presenting only two options when more exist.

label_guide.label: Ad Hominem
label_guide.description: Attacking the person making the argument rather than the argument itself.

label_guide.label: Equivocation
label_guide.description: Using a key term with two different meanings in the same argument.

label_guide.label: Circular Reasoning
label_guide.description: The conclusion is assumed in the premises (includes begging the question).

label_guide.label: Straw Man
label_guide.description: Distorting or exaggerating an opponent's position, then attacking that version.

label_guide.label: Red Herring
label_guide.description: Diverting attention to an irrelevant point instead of addressing the issue.

label_guide.label: Appeal to Ignorance
label_guide.description: Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false (or vice versa).

label_guide.label: Affirming the Consequent
label_guide.description: Formal fallacy: If P then Q; Q; therefore P.

label_guide.label: Denying the Antecedent
label_guide.description: Formal fallacy: If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q.

quiz.text: Since everyone in my class failed the test, clearly the teacher is incompetent and designed it unfairly, so my poor grade is completely unjustified.
quiz.label: Ad Hominem

quiz.text: Dr. Smith, a renowned physicist, claims that ghosts exist. Therefore, we must accept that ghosts are real because such an authority would not be wrong.
quiz.label: Appeal to Authority

quiz.text: The local bakery sells delicious croissants, so all bakeries in this country must have excellent pastries.
quiz.label: Hasty Generalization

quiz.text: Most teenagers prefer streaming music services over traditional radio, so streaming must be the superior audio format.
quiz.label: Bandwagon / Popularity

quiz.text: When choosing a pet, you must decide between getting a dog that requires daily walks or a cat that needs litter box cleaning—there are no other practical options for busy people.
quiz.label: False Dilemma

quiz.text: If we ban smoking in parks, next they'll ban eating in public, then ban talking outdoors, and eventually we'll lose all our freedoms. Therefore, we must oppose any smoking restrictions.
quiz.label: Slippery Slope

pairs.valid: Most climate scientists conclude that reducing methane emissions lowers near-term warming based on multi-decade atmospheric data.
pairs.fallacy: Most people think reducing methane emissions lowers near-term warming, so it must be true.

pairs.valid: Our survey indicates 60% support the policy, 30% oppose, and 10% are undecided.
pairs.fallacy: Everyone knows this policy is incredibly unpopular with normal people.

pairs.valid: The investment is risky, with volatility 40% above the market average.
pairs.fallacy: You shouldn't invest because it's too risky.

pairs.valid: The encryption is secure because it uses 256-bit AES, which remains unbroken by current computing power.
pairs.fallacy: This encryption method is safe because it provides security.

pairs.valid: The pedagogical method is effective, with students in the program outperforming controls on standardized assessments.
pairs.fallacy: This teaching style works because it helps students learn.

pairs.valid: This proposition is necessary because its negation leads to a logical contradiction.
pairs.fallacy: This must be true because it's necessarily the case.

pairs.valid: Data from 1,000 schools shows that free breakfast programs improve attendance by an average of 15%.
pairs.fallacy: The kids at my daughter's school still miss class, so free breakfast doesn't help.

pairs.valid: Extending the deadline for this project by one week accounts for the unexpected supply chain delay.
pairs.fallacy: If we extend this deadline once, soon every project will be delayed, deadlines will become meaningless, and our company will fail.
